speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) how does the Ministry ensure that wage increases in the Progressive Wage Model sectors are sustainable for employers given that wage increases may not be directly tied to productivity increases; and (b) given that wage growth will have to outpace productivity growth at the individual lower-wage worker level, whether the Government will consider providing support to businesses to enhance firm-level productivity such that businesses will be better able to support the wage increases for low-wage workers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) how will employers be able to verify the specific progressive wage that they need to pay their workers given the various sectors they come from; and (b) whether the verification process will form an onerous administrative burden on the employers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: asked the Minister for Manpower in light of the expanding coverage of the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) and new requirement for companies to pay all local employees at least the Local Qualifying Salary (a) whether any forms of support will be provided to consumers and businesses to manage cost increases; and (b) if so, what are they.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: asked the Minister for Manpower in light of the expanding coverage of the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) and new requirement for companies to pay all local employees at least the Local Qualifying Salary (LQS), how can the Ministry ensure that price increases purportedly resulting from the LQS will be fair, reasonable and not attempts at opportunistic profiteering.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: asked the Minister for Manpower how does the Ministry ensure that wage increases in the Progressive Wage Model sectors are sustainable for employers given that wage increases may not be directly tied to productivity increases.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: asked the Minister for Manpower with the proposed increase in wages for low-wage workers, how will the Ministry ensure that businesses do not profiteer under the pretext of having to pay higher wages.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) how is the Local Qualifying Salary being determined currently; and (b) how does the Ministry plan to review the monthly minimum salary regularly.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) how does the Ministry plan to inform and support employers to pay all local workers at least the Local Qualifying Salary to qualify for their employment of foreign workers; and (b) what will be the time period given to employers for this transition.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: asked the Minister for Manpower in view of increases in business costs with the implementation of the Progressive Wage Models (PWM), how will the Government (i) monitor that the increase in costs is fairly shared between the businesses and consumers and (ii) ensure that such cost increases will not raise the cost of living for the low wage workers such that the benefits of the PWM to them are outstripped.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Apart from my reply today, I would also like to encourage them to read the 88-page report of the Workgroup where the reasoning and intent of many of the proposals are laid out in greater detail.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Workgroup's vision is for a strengthened social compact where everyone enjoys Singapore's fruits of growth.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We want to enable our lower-wage workers to progress along with other workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the same time, society, employers and the Government stand in solidarity with them.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We must also recognise that, for our lower-wage workers’ progress to be sustainable, Singapore must maintain a dynamic economy, where businesses can thrive and create good jobs and good careers for our workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Uplifting lower-wage workers has been a priority for the Government over the years.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is a clear commitment that Workfare will continue to be a foundation of our policy response.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government will release more details next year.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workfare and Progressive Wages work in tandem and are, therefore, mutually reinforcing.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Over the last decade, our policies to support lower-wage workers have made a difference in uplifting them to enjoy good wage growth.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To address Ms Ng Ling Ling’s and Mr Desmond Choo’s questions, I want to stress that these are real income gains; in other words, 39% cumulative income gains, even after subtracting the effects of inflation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Low-income households would, therefore, benefit from our Progressive Wage and Workfare policies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I am sure many Members are aware that there are dedicated efforts to support our low-income households through various schemes, such as subsidies in education, healthcare, housing, as well as financial assistance.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Households facing financial difficulties can approach MSF’s Social Service Offices (SSOs), which will look into ways to support them through schemes, such as ComCare assistance.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: MSF regularly reviews ComCare to ensure that support remains adequate.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: First, we will expand Progressive Wages to new sectors like Food Services, Retail and Waste Management, as well as occupations like Administrators and Drivers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will also extend PWMs to in-house cleaners, security officers as well as landscape workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Third, we will introduce the Progressive Wage Mark, or PW Mark, to encourage firms that pay progressive wages.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Workgroup has not deviated from the broad principle that wages should grow in tandem with productivity over the long term, so as to be sustainable.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, it recognised that there was a case for wage growth of lower-wage workers to outpace productivity.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is because the productivity of frontline workers is not due solely to the industriousness of the worker, but it is also dependent on the firm’s operations and methods of work.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Workgroup also recommended that for the next decade, the wages of our lower-wage workers should continue to grow faster than the median, or what we call the "median-plus" approach.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, when wages at the 20th percentile have gained sufficiently on median wage levels, this would no longer be necessary.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We can reflect on other strategies beyond that.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Edward Chia and Mr Sharael Taha asked about the sustainability of these wage increases.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: One important way we will do this is to continue the Progressive Wage approach, whereby wage increases are secured by tripartite consensus, that is, the agreement between the employers and the unions remain very important.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These will be done by sectoral Tripartite Clusters for the Sectoral Progressive Wages, and the National Wages Council for the Occupational Progressive Wages.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I know for a fact, and especially during these times, that tripartite negotiations are never easy, and for good reason, as the concerns of different parties, of the employers and workers, need to be balanced.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Tripartism is our strength, and some say our secret sauce, to make Progressive Wages work for the foreseeable future.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I am confident that through such robust discussions, these established tripartite bodies will arrive at common ground that is sustainable and benefits all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If wage growth of our lower-wage workers outpace productivity growth in the medium term, the sustainable response is for businesses to use this period to urgently enhance their firm-level productivity to better support wage increases for our workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To Mr Sharael Taha’s query, the Government will continue to support firms through the Productivity Solutions Grant, as well as more specific efforts enabled by the Industry Transformation Maps.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For many years, firms hiring foreign workers have been required to pay at least the LQS to the local workers that they need to count towards their foreign worker quota, or Dependency Ratio Ceiling (DRC).

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is a policy that our businesses are already familiar with.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Workgroup studied this carefully and decided to leverage on the LQS to broaden our coverage of Progressive Wages.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This builds upon regular increases in the LQS level over the years, such as from $1,000 in 2016 to $1,400 in 2020.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But I would also like to take the opportunity to highlight that in 2020, many of our lower-wage workers were also impacted by the economic impact of COVID-19 and faced reduced work-hours and allowances.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These employees work in a wide range of industries, from Food Services to Administrative and Support Services, and occupy a diverse range of jobs, from cleaners to office clerks to shop sales assistants, and we can imagine the impact of COVID-19 on these jobs in the last year or year plus.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This was also why the Government provided special support of $3,000 to this segment of workers through the Workfare Special Payment and other social support schemes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Many in this group would also see their wages further uplifted beyond LQS, by the Sectoral and Occupational Progressive Wages.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Workgroup expects the PWMs to continue to set the pace on wage growth, with Progressive Wage levels expected to rise beyond the LQS.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For example, workers in the Cleaning and Landscape sectors can potentially earn at least about $2,400 a month by 2028.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To Ms Hazel Poa’s query, the remaining 23%, who are not covered, would be in businesses that do not hire foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The vast majority of these businesses are very small, hiring fewer than 10 workers and include small family operations, such as hawker stalls and heartland shops.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We are all familiar with these microbusinesses; they are familiar faces in our neighbourhoods and typically having family members who are spouses, children or relatives helping out.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: They do not have the business scale or reach, and we are mindful that sudden wage shifts to these microbusinesses can result in business failure.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, the last thing we want is for job losses for these family businesses.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: While not formally covered by the LQS requirement, these workers here should still see meaningful increases in their wages over time due to market forces.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, eight in 10 and moving up to 94%, I think we are quite confident that market forces will probably lift the remainder up over time.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Some Members, including Mr Yip Hon Weng, asked about how the LQS is currently being determined, and under what circumstances would it be reviewed.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As the Workgroup’s Report explains, the LQS is a stable benchmark that has been in place for many years.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It has been revised four times in the last five years.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We recognise that the new LQS requirement in 2022 will have a significant impact on employers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I urge Members not to look at each measure in isolation but to bear in mind the overall and holistic impact on not just the workers but also the employers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Members have also asked about the implementation details.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To Mr Edward Chia’s query, firms that hire foreign workers are already familiar with the concept of LQS for many years.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Together with tripartite partners, the Government will continue to reach out to firms before the new LQS requirement and other new Progressive Wages kick in on 1 September 2022.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The initial period beyond its introduction will be a run-in period, for which MOM will focus on educating employers on the various Progressive Wage and LQS requirements that they will need to adhere to.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In other words, I can assure employers that MOM will not jump straight into strict enforcement, but it will initially focus on improving awareness and compliance, because we are all moving towards a new system.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is the same approach that was adopted when new Employment Act obligations were introduced in 2016.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In designing the system to support the new moves, we will make the compliance process as smooth as possible.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To Miss Rachel Ong’s query, we will keep additional reporting requirements minimal by tapping on existing processes such as CPF salary declarations and returns to MOM’s Business Census.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Employers will also be able to refer to MOM’s website to check the job descriptions of workers eligible for Progressive Wages and the required wages.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will also explore ways to allow employees to check that they are paid the Progressive Wages due to them.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, employees also have a chance to get used to the new system.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We note that the Singapore Business Federation has acknowledged that the Report of the Workgroup has taken into consideration their feedback on minimising the burden of compliance for firms.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To Mr Liang Eng Hwa’s query on how the PW Mark will be administered, we will tap on the same systems that I have just described, to ensure that only firms that pay Progressive Wages are awarded the PW Mark.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This will assure companies and consumers that when they purchase from firms with the PW Mark, they are directly supporting the lower-wage workers in these firms.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As the support of private sector buyers is also essential, the tripartite partners will also work with the various trade associations and chambers to raise awareness of the PW Mark, promote its adoption and encourage businesses to purchase from other businesses with the PW Mark.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, workers will have to adopt the right mindset and be ready to adapt and learn new skills to be more productive.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Employers will need to increase productivity at the firm-level, which would help them better absorb the additional wage costs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: With respect to employers, the Government recognises that employers will need some time to adjust their operations, especially as the economy is still recovering from COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government is committed to Workfare as a permanent scheme; at the same time, employers do their part by offering progressive wages.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Miss Rachel Ong asked why we are lowering the Workfare qualifying age to 30 years old and whether we will lower it further below the age of 30.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Below the age of 30, most workers would have just started work and earning starting salaries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Most will have greater potential for future income growth.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, it will be too premature to consider them for Workfare.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: They could be better supported through training and upskilling efforts, such as SkillsFuture, to help them access better jobs and grow their wages in a sustainable way.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For workers aged 30 to 34, however, some continued to remain in the lower-wage range despite the upskilling efforts.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At this age, they are just starting their own families or are looking to buy their first home.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We believe that Workfare will help them better cope with their current expenses and to start saving for their retirement.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui and other Members asked if businesses will unfairly raise prices.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I can certainly understand why this is a big concern for many of us.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In the Food Services and Retail sectors, where there are many firms competing and barriers to entry are not high, firms will be expected to think carefully about cost increases.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is also fair to say that we have to expect some degree of cost increase to accommodate higher salaries for our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is where we, as consumers, have to do our part in support of our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I, therefore, hope that Singaporeans will not accuse firms unfairly of profiteering, but let us also work together to address any unreasonable price increases or practices.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: One reason why the Workgroup recommended that the National Wages Council help to provide guidance on wage growth is to enable the tripartite partners to carefully weigh the impact of wage growth, inflation and general economic conditions every year, before finalising their guidance.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Because the growth of Progressive Wages is negotiated through tripartite consensus, rest assured we have more assurance that wage increases will be sustainable for workers, employers as well as consumers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To do this well, we will need to go beyond a whole-of-Government approach, or even a whole-of-tripartite sector approach.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will need the whole of society – workers, consumers, employers, unions, the Government, members of the public – to come behind and support this effort.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Tripartite partners have agreed on a roadmap to chart the progress of our lower-wage workers over the next decade.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And many businesses and consumers already recognise that they will need to do their part by paying a little more for goods and services.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There has been heartening support from society at large since the Prime Minister spoke at the National Day Rally.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I would also like to thank the tripartite partners for helping chart this roadmap ahead.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, let us continue on this course, to bring society together behind the goal of supporting our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I understand the need for LQS and the intent to uplift the wages of lower-wage workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Senior Minister of State did talk about the need for PWMs to complement that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am concerned, however, and I am asking the Senior Minister of State how do we ensure that LQS does not become the maximum wage for lower-wage workers in companies that hire foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In fact, as I have shared earlier, the main driver of wage growth in the next decade or so will really be your PWMs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It has been heartening to see how employers have come on board despite the last one year being a challenging year with COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And if you look at the PWMs that were renewed for the next six, eight years, you will see in the cleaning and landscape sectors how employers have supported us through this and grown the wage ladders at a pace that is faster than the median, in what we call the median-plus approach.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These are ways in which we support them and these will drive market forces, too.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Speaking to employers, I know some are also concerned that if a cleaner, for example, earns $2,400 a month in 2028, then the rest in the firm will also seek to ask, "Why not the tea lady?" and the tea lady asking "Why am I not earning the same as a cleaner?" and administrators, for example, doing so.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, these are areas in which I think will be game changers in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But at the same time, the concern of some parts of society is whether this will also increase costs for businesses.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, that is also the other part where we will see how to balance this.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On LQS, this is a measure that most employers are already quite familiar with.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, we have seen many of them having their income drop.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is where we think, in the long term, this PWM will help them over time and in a sustainable manner because the employers are all on board with us on this.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, look forward to some of the upcoming PWMs – food services, retail, waste management – which will come on from next year onwards.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The tripartite clusters are negotiating the wage benchmarks.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: They will come up to share what these new benchmarks will be.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And occupational progressive wages across sectors for administrators as well as the drivers are also key to us and something that we are now still negotiating and we will come up with the benchmarks soon, too.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, looking at all these wage benchmarks and wage ladders ahead, I am quite confident that the PWMs will continue to drive wage growth.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But at the same time, it is important that we assure employers that these moves are sustainable.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I am glad that most are on board and supporting us on this, despite the challenging times today.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On top of that, I have two supplementary questions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would this spell the end of part-time employment?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last question: the Senior Minister of State mentioned that over the years 2009 to 2019, the real wage growth of the lowest quintile outperformed those of the highest.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we look at only wage growth, it does not include other incomes like investment income or rental income.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, this does not quite give us the full picture of how inequality is changing.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does MOM track similar data but in terms of total income?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, it is about 20%, or 20,000 or thereabouts.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And as I have shared, with progressive wages, you will end up, hopefully, covering up to 94% of our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: You will see the long-term impact in terms of how their wages will grow over time.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Also, bear in mind that the remainder that is left are typically those in microbusinesses.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Like I have shared, in heartland shops, they are people you are very familiar with and the last thing you want is to have them collapse in the short term because they do not have the scale.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And many of them are uncles and aunties running stalls and I am not even sure whether the uncle pays the auntie full wages.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But these are areas in which I think we have to correct over time, but you do not want to collapse them in the short term.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, this is something we are very mindful not to disrupt the whole system in such a way.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We also give you half a count for DRC if you employ at least half of the LQS rate, that is, $700 a month for part-timers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, this is one way in which we still maintain the current system but, at the same time, provide some flexibility for part-time workers, for many of our employees.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That one, employers do not have to worry too much because they are familiar with the system and the part-time mechanism still continues.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is just that we now set a $9 rate per hour for part-time workers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With regard to firms' level of productivity, are there actually specific plans to ensure that firm-level productivity support dovetails with worker upskilling and not as two separate activities?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second supplementary question is with regard to LQS.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can the Ministry consider a predictable timeline for future adjustments so that employers can make reasonable financial projections, especially when they are entering or pricing fixed-price term tenders?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Two things: one, let me just start with the LQS.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think I have shared earlier that the Government's approach is that we will start with reaching out to firms and getting them familiar with this new LQS requirement.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: With this change, I think it affects many of our businesses, so it is important that we give them time to run in.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But I am quite sure firms are already quite familiar with this LQS mechanism.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That is why this was an ideal framework to leverage on, because it is not something new that firms have not complied with in the past.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is just that the framework has been modified and tweaked.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On the second question on firm level productivity and workers' productivity, that is a very good question.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To some extent, the narrative with many of our firms today and the approach so far with PWM has been that workers have to upskill and improve productivity.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, they have to justify productivity gains against wage gains.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But moving forward, we also have to think about productivity gains very differently, too.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There is the worker level productivity as you train and upskill him, but there is also that level of productivity leap that you can get when firms make the effort to transform, do job redesigns.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Like the securities sector, for example, when you think of a security guard in the old days, you think of a "jaga" at the gate.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If you just train him that way, there is only so much productivity you can gain with him as a jaga at the gate.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But I have to commend the security sector.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Through PWM and working with the unions in the sector, I am quite heartened today that they are using CCTVs, technologies, and you see, suddenly, the firm level productivity jumps.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, if you look at the wage levels of our security officers, they have also jumped in the last five years.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, that justifies productivity, not just at the worker level, but because businesses also push on with the transformation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think if you look at many other sectors, including cleaning and landscape, we are seeing them make those changes, making efforts towards job redesign and transformation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That is also why firms were agreeable to the wage increases that we have seen in terms of the wage ladders in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Because they also bear in mind how contracts will be in the near future and how we are moving towards outcome-based contracting.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These are ways in which they can offer more, use better technologies, look at how we can redesign jobs to make them more attractive.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have seen entry rates of locals into these jobs increase.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Many of us have also seen appeals at Meet-the-People Sessions where there are more locals today asking for security licences because they know that the wages are much better today and, therefore, worth considering.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is one way in which when you look at productivity gains, in terms of wages, it should not just be on the basis of the worker level productivity but this is where the Government continues to support through our Productivity Solutions Grant and Industry Transformation Maps to make sure that our companies are able to transform and redesign the jobs to be more productive and pay our workers better salaries and give them better careers too.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, it is merely a coincidence that the LQS of $1,400 is similar to the average household expenditure on basic needs (AHEBN) for the bottom 20% of income earners.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As such, would it not be better to peg the minimum wage to the AHEBN instead of the LQS?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will allow the minimum wage to rise in tandem with cost increases so that the low-wage workers will not lose out over time.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But it has been adjusted because we have got various wage benchmarks that we work on.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The main goal of the LQS was also to ensure that Singaporeans' wages were not depressed as we hire foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, as we hire foreign workers using a Singaporean for the quota, we did not want the Singaporean worker to be left out and be depressed because you, typically, would have access to cheaper foreign labour out there.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Of course, we have other obligations made on the employer, such as taking care of the worker, giving him food if he is in a dormitory and so forth, and medical expenses.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But overall, I think, net-net, the objective was not to have Singaporeans lose out, as firms access foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Unlike minimum wage laws around the world, there is the International Labour Convention where you cannot have laws that discriminate between locals and foreigners.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, for most legislation around the world, you will find minimum wages covering both local and foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This enables us to make a differentiation, but the overall concept still applies, whereby as you hire foreign workers in your firm, you want to ensure that not just those that are being counted have a fair wage, but every Singaporean worker in your firm has a fair wage too.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The last thing you want is to have a political auction on what the wage level should be.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But let us pick a fair one, where a committee looks at available data projections and see what is sustainable, and the impact to inflation because that too, is a concern for many Singaporeans – cost of living over time.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These are quite complex matters which we need to give assurance, not just to the workers but to the employers and the consumers at large too, to create a fair system.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the same time, as I have shared, it also gives us a release valve for many of our microbusinesses who are not currently part of the LQS because they are, typically, your heartland shops and many of these micro-businesses recruit less than 10 workers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How would the Ministry help companies that are locked into forward contracts with their customers, like those in the construction sector, to bear the additional cost of the LQS requirement?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For cleaning, security and landscape, for example, these are also contracts that run three to five years ahead.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, we announce it today for a new PWM ladder that starts in 2023, for example.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is one way in which we help firms prepare and we give them advance notice.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The sector also understands this, that we, typically, give them advance headway to do this.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For the short term, as I have said, look out for our announcements on the transition support before the new LQS requirements and PWMs kick in next year.
